# IntoMind One documentation

<!-- https://docs.intomind.com/index.html -->

# IntoMind™ One

IntoMind One is a research grade EEG device that you wear. It streams four channels of your brain's electrical activity to your computer over Bluetooth, and the software that records, analyzes and builds on it is open.

## Start here

| | |
|---|---|
| [The device](https://docs.intomind.com/device.html) | what is in the box, charging, wearing it, the lights, and connecting |
| [Command Center](https://docs.intomind.com/command-center.html) | the app for seeing the signal, recording, and exporting |
| [Python](https://docs.intomind.com/python.html) | the API, for scripts, recordings and analysis |
| [Recordings and files](https://docs.intomind.com/files.html) | what a recording is, what each export holds, and the rule versions follow |
| [Rust](https://docs.intomind.com/rust.html) and [JavaScript](https://docs.intomind.com/javascript.html) | the SDK, for building your own applications |
| [MicroPython](https://docs.intomind.com/micropython.html) | MicroPython for the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W, for programs that run on the board |
| [The model and heads](https://docs.intomind.com/model.html) | the neural network on the device, and training your own heads |
| [The protocol](https://docs.intomind.com/protocol.html) | the Bluetooth contract, for writing your own client |
| [Safety and care](https://docs.intomind.com/safety.html) | warnings, the battery, and cleaning |
| [Glossary](https://docs.intomind.com/glossary.html) | the terms used on this site |

## How it works

![The signal from the scalp to your computer](https://docs.intomind.com/assets/img/signal-path.svg)

Four electrodes and a reference rest on the scalp. The ADC converts what they pick up into 24-bit samples, at 250, 500 or 1000 samples per second, and the device stamps each sample with its own clock. The device filters the signal through a processing chain you can read and change, and every stream states the chain that produced it. If a sample is lost on the way, the stream says where and how many. Nothing is filled in.

The device also runs a neural network that describes every 4 seconds of signal with 76 numbers. You can train heads on those numbers and run them on the device. In place of the electrodes, a generator on the device can stream a synthetic signal, marked as generated wherever it goes.

## What you need

A computer with Bluetooth Low Energy. The Command Center runs on it and shows its page in your browser. Once installed, it needs no account and no internet connection.

## Open source

The Command Center, the API, the SDK, the `intomind` library for MicroPython and the open heads are free software under the [GNU Affero General Public License, version 3](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.html). For a commercial license, write to contact@intomind.com.

| | |
|---|---|
| [github.com/intomind/commandcenter](https://github.com/intomind/commandcenter) | the Command Center |
| [github.com/intomind/api](https://github.com/intomind/api) | the Python API, `pip install 'intomind[analysis]'` |
| [github.com/intomind/sdk](https://github.com/intomind/sdk) | the SDK, `cargo add intomind` and `npm install @intomind/sdk` |
| [github.com/intomind/micropython](https://github.com/intomind/micropython) | MicroPython for the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W, with the `intomind` library |
| [github.com/intomind/eeg-foundation-model-heads](https://github.com/intomind/eeg-foundation-model-heads) | the open heads for the model on the device |

<!-- https://docs.intomind.com/device.html -->

# The device

**IntoMind One (IM-1)**

## What is in the box

- The IntoMind One, assembled and programmed, in its 3D printed enclosure, with its rechargeable battery and comfort strap.
- A T-shirt in the size you chose at checkout.

A charging cable is not included.

## Charging

> **Warning.** To ensure safety, never wear the device or touch its electrodes while USB is plugged in.

Plug a USB-C cable into any USB charger or computer. The charge light shows what the charger is doing. Charging from empty takes about an hour and three quarters, and a full charge streams for about 25 hours.

While USB is plugged in, the device charges and stays connected, but it does not stream from its electrodes. A stream cannot be started, and a stream that is running stops when the cable goes in. The [synthetic signal](#the-synthetic-signal) still streams.

## Turning it on and off

Slide the power switch to turn the device on. The amber power light is lit while the device is on, and your computer can find it.

The battery drains slowly even while the device is off, so charge it before you store it.

## Wearing it

The electrodes must touch skin, not hair. Part the hair where each electrode sits, and press the device down until the electrodes rest on the scalp. The comfort strap holds it in place and lets you place the electrodes anywhere on the head. It should feel firm but not tight.

A noisy channel almost always means poor contact. Lift the device, part the hair again, and press it back down. If every channel is noisy, check the reference electrode.

The Command Center can turn on lead-off detection, which shows which electrodes are in contact with the skin. It passes a very small current through the electrodes, so it stays off until you turn it on.

## The lights

| Light | Color | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| Power | amber | lit while the device is on |
| Charge | yellow, magenta or red | lit only while USB is plugged in: yellow while charging, magenta when full, red when no battery is connected |
| Status | amber | what the device is doing, in the patterns below |

The status light has three settings: silent, reserved and verbose. The device ships set to reserved and keeps its setting when it is turned off. The Command Center sets it under the device's settings.

| Pattern | Meaning | Shown in |
|---|---|---|
| Lit, with a short dark wink once a second | your software asked this device to identify itself | every setting |
| Three blinks, then a pause | the ADC failed its check at power on, so the device cannot record | reserved and verbose |
| Two blinks, then a pause | the battery is below 20 percent, until it reaches 25 percent or USB is plugged in | reserved and verbose |
| Fast blinking | an update is being written | verbose |
| A brief pulse every two seconds | streaming | verbose |
| Steady | connected | verbose |
| A short blink once a second | on, and waiting for a computer | verbose |

When more than one applies, the light shows the one highest in the table.

## Connecting

Turn the device on and connect from the [Command Center](https://docs.intomind.com/command-center.html) or your own software. The first time, your computer pairs with the device, with no code to enter. After that it connects without pairing again. The link is encrypted.

The device remembers four computers. When a fifth pairs, it forgets the one used least recently.

## Several devices at once

One computer can stream from two devices at 250 samples per second each. At 500 or 1000 samples per second, stream from one device per computer.

## Its name

The device can carry a name and an adjective that you choose, and every computer and phone that scans for Bluetooth devices sees them with the product's name: Ada's Blue IntoMind One. With only a name it is Ada's IntoMind One, with only an adjective Blue IntoMind One, and with neither IntoMind One. The device keeps them when it is turned off, and a new name appears in scans once the computer that set it disconnects.

The whole name is at most 29 bytes. English letters, digits and spaces take one byte each. Accented letters and other scripts take two to four.

When two devices near your computer have the same name, the software numbers the second one: Ada's IntoMind One 2. The number exists only on your computer.

## The synthetic signal

The device can stream a signal it generates itself, in place of its electrodes, to test software without anyone wearing it and for demonstrations. It runs at 500 samples per second, and every packet and recording of it is marked as generated. The Command Center says so above the trace.

The device runs one neural network at a time. While it generates the signal, it sends no embeddings and no predictions, and it does not start generating while either is on.

The generator draws the encoder's tokens, and the reconstruction head turns them back into signal. Compared with 19,459 windows of real EEG from 37 studies it was not trained on:

| | Synthetic | Real EEG |
|---|---|---|
| A linear classifier on the encoder's embeddings, telling generated from real (0.5 means it cannot tell) | 0.56 | 0.38 to 0.58, between real studies |
| The same classifier, trained and scored on studies the generator never saw | 0.64 | |
| A nonlinear classifier on the same embeddings | 1.00, it always tells them apart | |
| Power spectrum, 1 to 45 Hz | 1.5 dB from real EEG on average | |
| Coherence between channels, 8 to 13 Hz | 0.18 | 0.28 |

The generator was trained with the encoder in the loop, so the first result is partly by design. The signal describes no one and varies less over time than a real person does. Use it to test software, never as data.

## Firmware updates

Firmware updates install over Bluetooth. The device keeps two copies of its firmware, writes an update to the copy it is not running, and runs only firmware signed by IntoMind. If your computer cannot connect after an update, turn the device off and on. If it still cannot connect, turn it off and on once more, and the device returns to the previous firmware.

## If something is wrong

| What you see | What to do |
|---|---|
| It does not appear in a scan | Check that the power light is on. If it is not, charge the device. |
| One channel is noisy | Improve that electrode's contact: lift the device, part the hair, and press it down. |
| Every channel is noisy | Improve the reference electrode's contact. |
| A stream will not start, or stops | Unplug USB. The device does not stream from its electrodes while USB is plugged in. |
| It disconnects | Move the computer closer, and away from other devices on the same radio band. |
| It connects but never answers, or a feature is missing after an update | Remove the device in your computer's Bluetooth settings (on Linux, `bluetoothctl remove` and its address) and connect again. |
| Three blinks | Turn the device off and on. If it happens again, write to support@intomind.com. |
| The Command Center says another program is listening | Another program on this computer is subscribed to the device, so every packet arrives twice. The copies are dropped and the recording is complete. |

## Specifications

| | |
|---|---|
| Channels | 4, with a shared reference |
| Electrodes | five, dry and gold-plated |
| ADC | Texas Instruments ADS1299-4, 24 bits |
| Sample rates | 250, 500 or 1000 per second |
| Gain | 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12 or 24 |
| Noise | 0.14 µV root mean square, inputs shorted, at 250 samples per second |
| Timestamps | every sample, from the device's own clock |
| Processing | high-pass, notch and low-pass filters on the device, which you can read and set |
| Model | an encoder that describes each 4-second window with 76 numbers, and four slots for your heads |
| Radio | Raytac MDBT50Q-1MV2 module, Nordic nRF52840 |
| Link | Bluetooth Low Energy, encrypted |
| Battery | rechargeable lithium polymer, charged over USB-C |
| Lights | power, charge and status |
| Enclosure | 3D printed bioplastic, with an adjustable comfort strap |

## What the IntoMind One supports

The [protocol](https://docs.intomind.com/protocol.html) covers every IntoMind device, and each device reports which parts it supports.

| Feature | IntoMind One |
|---|---|
| Streaming at three rates and seven gains, the ADC's test signal and shorted inputs, lead-off detection, time sync | yes |
| Battery and charger state | yes |
| Signed firmware updates over Bluetooth | yes |
| The processing chain: read, set, clear, and restore the default | yes |
| The model: embeddings, heads, predictions, and how often it runs | yes |
| The status light: its setting, and identify | yes |
| The ADC's registers, read while not streaming | yes |
| Its name | yes |
| The synthetic signal | yes, at 500 samples per second |
| The bias drive | no |

<!-- https://docs.intomind.com/command-center.html -->

# Command Center

The Command Center is the app for using an IntoMind One from your computer. It runs a small server on your computer and shows its page in your browser, where you connect to the device, watch the signal, record, and export.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/intomind/commandcenter
cd commandcenter
pip install 'intomind[analysis]' aiohttp
python3 hub.py
```

Then open http://localhost:8080. It needs Python 3.11 or newer. The page also works with no device connected, so you can review recordings anywhere. On Linux, `./install-launcher.sh` adds it to your applications.

## What it does

- Lists the devices it hears and connects only the one you pick. It shows the device's firmware, channels and protocol version.
- Shows the live signal, and which electrodes are in contact when lead-off detection is on.
- Records, with markers or with cued protocols such as eyes open and closed, blinks, jaw clenches and eye movements.
- Reads recordings back, runs analyses on them, and exports them.
- Selects a head on the device and shows its predictions, sets how often the model runs, and saves the model's embeddings to a file for training heads.
- Sets the status light and the device's name, and makes the device identify itself.
- Says above the trace whenever the signal does not come from the electrodes, and when another program on the computer is also listening to the device.

The page has three levels. Basic shows every setting and lets you change a few everyday ones. Intermediate also lets you change the device's settings and its processing chain, and shows the ADC's registers. Advanced also lets you change the signal source and the analysis settings.

## Recordings

Recordings are saved in the `captures` folder inside the Command Center's folder, and exports in `exports`. A recording holds its samples, its events, and a record of how it was made: the device and its firmware, its settings, the processing chain, whether the signal was measured or generated, and where any gaps are. Checksums are written last, so a recording that stopped partway is never mistaken for a complete one.

## Exports

| Format | |
|---|---|
| BDF | 24-bit biosignal format, every value kept |
| EDF | the older 16-bit format, rounded to 16 bits |
| npz | NumPy arrays |
| CSV and TSV | text tables |
| MATLAB | version 7.3 files, every value kept |

Each export reports whether every value came out exactly as recorded, and if not, the largest error in microvolts. A recording whose checksums do not match is not exported. The Command Center uses the Python API's exporters, so a file exported here matches one exported from a script.

In BDF and EDF every sample stays at the time it was recorded. Where samples were lost, the file fills the hole with a placeholder that repeats the last recorded value and labels it `BAD_ACQ_SKIP`, which MNE reads as a gap, and the page says how many samples it filled. A program that does not know the label shows a hole as a flat line. These files are made of whole blocks of about a second, and the last block is completed after the last sample the same way, so no recorded sample is left out, and the page says how many placeholders that took. What every file holds and promises is on [Recordings and files](https://docs.intomind.com/files.html).

Every format carries electrode contact where detection was on during the recording, and only there, because a reading of "attached" means nothing when nothing was checking. CSV and TSV add a column per channel: 1 where the electrode was off, 0 where it was attached, and empty where detection was off. BDF and EDF label each stretch an electrode was off `BAD_LEADOFF`, which MNE treats as bad. The page says whether contact was checked. A recording made before this was kept says it is not known.

## It answers only your computer

The server listens only on your own computer, and it refuses requests from web pages on other sites, so a page you visit cannot reach it. The page loads nothing from the internet.

## License

Free software under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3. For a commercial license, write to contact@intomind.com.

<!-- https://docs.intomind.com/python.html -->

# Python

The `intomind` package is the Python API for the IntoMind One. It connects to the device, streams its signal, and reads, exports and analyzes recordings. The [Command Center](https://docs.intomind.com/command-center.html) is built on it.

```sh
pip install 'intomind[analysis]'
```

It needs Python 3.11 or newer. The `analysis` extra installs SciPy, which reading recordings, exporting and the analyses need. For MATLAB export, install `'intomind[analysis,mat]'`.

```python
import asyncio

from intomind.client import display_names, scan
from intomind.session import Session


async def main():
    found = await scan()                       # every device that answered
    names = display_names(found)               # address to name, numbered when two share one
    device = next(d for d in found if names[d.address] == "Ada's IntoMind One")

    session = Session()
    await session.connect(device)              # only the device you picked
    device = session.devices[0]

    device.on_sample = lambda dev, sample: print(sample.index, sample.uv)
    await device.start()
    await asyncio.sleep(5)
    await device.stop()
    await session.close()


asyncio.run(main())
```

Each sample carries the device's index (`sample.index`), the device time at which it was converted (`sample.device_time`), that time on your computer's clock (`sample.host_time`), and one value per channel in microvolts (`sample.uv`).

The first connection pairs the device with your computer, and later connections reuse the pairing. On Linux the library answers the pairing request itself, so no settings window is needed and a computer without a screen works. If a connection fails because the link could not be secured, the error says what to do.

## What the device reports

The library holds no table of hardware. What a device can do is what it reports, and a request for anything else is refused before it is sent, with an error that names the missing capability.

```python
device.info.channels          # 4
device.info.adc_bits          # 24
device.info.rates             # the sample rates it offers
device.can("model")           # True when it reports that capability
```

## Processing on the device

The device filters its signal through a chain you can read and change, and only the chain's output streams. The device refuses changes while it streams: stop, set, and start again.

```python
from intomind import protocol

state = await device.pipeline()                        # the chain in force
await device.set_pipeline([protocol.highpass(0.5),
                           *protocol.mains_bands(60, 500),  # 60 Hz and the harmonics 500 per second can carry
                           protocol.lowpass()])        # the automatic corner
await device.restore_pipeline_default()
await device.clear_pipeline()                          # no processing
```

A chain that cannot run at the device's rate is refused, with the reason, before anything is sent.

## The light, the name, and the registers

```python
await device.set_indicator("verbose")       # "silent", "reserved" or "verbose"
await device.identify(5)                    # the status light winks for five seconds

await device.set_name("Ada", "Blue")        # refused if the whole name would not fit
protocol.compose_name("Ada", "Blue")        # "Ada's Blue IntoMind One"

regs = await device.converter_registers()   # the ADC's registers, while not streaming
regs.describe()                             # its settings, in words
```

## The synthetic signal

```python
await device.set_mode("synthetic")          # the generator, at 500 samples per second
await device.set_mode("normal")             # back to the electrodes
```

Turn embeddings and predictions off first, because the device runs one neural network at a time. Every generated sample has `sample.synthetic` set. See [the device](https://docs.intomind.com/device.html#the-synthetic-signal) for what the signal is.

## The model

This example collects four minutes of embeddings with eyes open and four with eyes closed, trains a head that tells them apart, and runs it on the device.

```python
from intomind.model import train_head

await device.start()
opened = await device.collect_embeddings(60, form="window")    # 60 windows, 4 minutes, eyes open
closed = await device.collect_embeddings(60, form="window")    # eyes closed

head = train_head([w.embedding for w in opened + closed],
                  [0] * len(opened) + [1] * len(closed),
                  name="eyes closed", encoder_id=opened[0].encoder_id)

await device.upload_head(head, slot=2, select=True)
device.on_prediction = lambda dev, p: print(p.outputs)
await device.set_predictions(True)
```

[The model and heads](https://docs.intomind.com/model.html) explains embeddings, heads, and how often the model runs.

## Gaps and repeated packets

```python
from intomind import analysis

capture = analysis.load("my-recording")    # checks the checksums first
capture.gap_before                         # one flag per sample: True where samples were lost before it
capture.meta["synthetic"]                  # True when the device generated the signal
```

The device numbers every sample, so a loss has an exact count. When the device restarts its count, the library reports a break of unknown length, never a count.

When another program on the same computer listens to the device, every packet arrives twice. The library drops the copies and counts them in `device.duplicates`.

## Where recordings go

```python
from intomind import provenance

provenance.use_captures_dir("~/study/captures")
provenance.use_site({"mains_hz": 60, "electrode_montage": "four over the forehead"})
```

Recordings go to `~/.local/share/intomind/captures` unless `INTOMIND_CAPTURES` or `use_captures_dir` names another folder. `use_site` records facts about where you record. Anything you do not declare is recorded as unknown.

## Exports

```python
from intomind import export

export.export("my-recording", "bdf")       # also "edf", "npz", "csv", "tsv" and "mat"
```

Each export reports whether every value came out exactly as recorded, and if not, the largest error in microvolts. A recording whose checksums do not match is refused.

In BDF and EDF, every sample stays at the time it was recorded. Where samples were lost, the file holds one placeholder for each of them, repeating the last recorded value, under a `BAD_ACQ_SKIP` annotation that MNE reads as its own, so MNE leaves the hole out of filtering and returns it as NaN when asked. A reader that does not know the label shows a hole as a flat line. The files are whole blocks of about a second, and the last block is completed after the last sample the same way, so no recorded sample is left out. `export.export` reports how many placeholders it wrote in `samples_filled` and `tail_filled`. What every file holds and promises is on [Recordings and files](https://docs.intomind.com/files.html).

Lead-off is in every format, and only where the recording says detection was running, because a lead-off status of zero is an attached electrode there and nothing at all anywhere else. CSV and TSV add a `chN_leadoff` column per channel: 1 where the electrode was off, 0 where it was attached, and empty where nothing was checking. BDF and EDF label each stretch an electrode was off `BAD_LEADOFF` and the channel, which MNE treats as bad. NPZ and MATLAB hold the flag itself as `leadoff_active`. Every export reports in `contact` whether contact was checked, and a recording made before the flag was kept reports "not known".

## Analyses

```python
analysis.summary("my-recording")           # offset, noise, band power, spectral slope
analysis.psd_curve("my-recording")         # the power spectrum of every channel
analysis.berger("my-recording")            # alpha with eyes closed against eyes open
```

## Other hardware

An adapter, in a package of its own, adds methods under `device.extra` for the devices it claims. A device without one behaves as documented here. See `adapters.py` in the [repository](https://github.com/intomind/api).

# Recordings and files

Every recording made with the Command Center, the Python API or the Rust crates is kept the same way, and every export follows the same rules, whichever program asked for it. The Rust crates and the JavaScript package read the same recordings and write the same six files, byte for byte or array for array, as [Rust](https://docs.intomind.com/rust.html#recordings-and-exports) and [JavaScript](https://docs.intomind.com/javascript.html#recordings-and-exports) show. This page is the contract: what a recording is, what each file holds, and what will not change.

## A recording

A recording is a set of files that share one name, in the recordings folder (`captures` by default).

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `name.npz` | The samples, as the converter's own counts for every channel, with each sample's index, device time and host time, and the lead-off byte and gap mark that arrived with it. |
| `name.meta.json` | The manifest: when the recording was made, the device and its firmware, its settings, the processing chain, whether the signal was measured or generated, where any gaps are, the electrode positions when they were given, and a version number for the manifest itself. |
| `name.events.json` | The markers placed during the recording, each at its device time. |
| `name.sha256` | A checksum of every file above, written last. |

Four things hold for every recording:

- The checksums are written last. A recording without them stopped partway, and no export or analysis treats it as complete.
- A recording is never rewritten. A fact learned later, such as where the electrodes were, is kept in a separate file beside it, so what the instrument recorded and what a person added afterwards stay distinguishable.
- A manifest field is never renamed, and every older manifest version stays readable. New fields are added and old ones keep their meaning.
- The samples are the record. Every other file, including every export, is derived from them and can be made again.

## Exports

```python
from intomind import export

export.export("my-recording", "bdf")       # also "edf", "npz", "csv", "tsv" and "mat"
```

Six formats, one call. Every one refuses a recording whose checksums do not match. Every one reports the same six things, `label`, `path`, `format`, `channels`, `samples` and `sample_rate_hz`, and whether every value came out exactly as recorded. Where a value could not, `lossy` is true and `max_error_uv` is the largest error in microvolts.

| Format | What it holds |
|---|---|
| npz | Microvolts per channel as `ch1_uv` and so on, with each sample's index, device time, host time, lead-off byte and gap mark, and the manifest. Every value as recorded. |
| csv and tsv | One header row, then one row per sample: `host_time_s`, `device_time`, and a microvolt column per channel. The rows are the samples, in order, and nothing is inserted where samples were lost. Both clocks are there so that a gap shows in the text. |
| mat | MATLAB version 7.3, which needs `h5py`. The microvolts as `uv`, the manifest as one line of text, and the per-sample arrays. Every value as recorded. |
| bdf | BDF+, 24 bits per sample. At 24 bits the step is narrower than one converter count on any recording that does not span the whole converter, so the values are what was recorded and the error is measured, not assumed. |
| edf | EDF+, 16 bits per sample, and therefore lossy by construction. `max_error_uv` says by how much. The step depends on the signal's own range in the file, not on its offset. |

A recording the device generated is marked as generated wherever it goes: the columns are named `ch1_synthetic_uv`, the MATLAB matrix `synthetic_uv`, and the manifest says so.

In a MATLAB file written by 1.4.1 or earlier, the manifest opens as a column of characters. `jsondecode(S.manifest_json(:)')` reads it from a file of any version.

## Time in BDF and EDF files

In BDF and EDF, every sample is written at the time it was recorded, counted from the sample index the device gave it. This is what the files promise, and what changed in 1.4.1.

- **A hole** holds one placeholder for every sample that was lost, so everything after it stays where it belongs, under a `BAD_ACQ_SKIP` annotation over exactly the hole. That is the label MNE gives a hole in its own files: it filters each side of a hole separately, rejects an epoch that overlaps one, and returns the hole as NaN when asked with `get_data(reject_by_annotation="NaN")`. A reader that does not know the label shows a hole as a flat line.
- **The placeholder** repeats the last recorded value, which is what MNE's own writer puts in the block it completes. These formats hold whole numbers, so NaN cannot be written. A value apart from the signal, such as the lowest number the file can store, is a step thousands of microvolts deep that a filter or a spectrum takes for signal. The last value adds no step and costs no precision, because it is already inside the signal's range.
- **The last block.** The files are whole blocks of about a second, and the last block is completed after the last sample with the same placeholder under the same label, so no recorded sample and no marker is left out. Before 1.4.1, the samples after the last whole block were left out of the file and counted in `samples_dropped`. That key is still reported, and is now 0.
- **A restart.** A recording whose sample count starts again within its first second begins with samples from before the recording started. The file starts at the restart, and `samples_before_restart` says how many samples were left out. A count that steps back later is a break whose length is not known, and the file is refused rather than given a timeline the recording does not have.
- **The sample rate** is kept exactly. The device's measured rate is rarely a whole number, and these formats need a whole number of samples per block, so the block's duration carries the remainder.
- **The range** each signal states in the header is rounded outward, so its lowest and highest samples are never clipped.
- **Markers** are written as annotations at their recorded times.

What these two exports report, beyond the six things every export reports:

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `gaps` | how many holes the file has |
| `samples_filled` | how many placeholders fill them |
| `tail_filled` | how many placeholders complete the last block |
| `samples_before_restart` | how many samples before a restart were left out |
| `samples_dropped` | how many recorded samples were left out of the file, 0 since 1.4.1 |
| `continuity` | `+C` for a continuous file |
| `bits`, `quantum_uv`, `lsb_uv` | the sample width, the file's step in microvolts, and the recording's own step |

## Lead-off in files

Lead-off detection reports which electrodes have come off, and it runs only when it is turned on. A lead-off reading of zero means every electrode was attached only while detection ran, so every file carries lead-off only where the recording says detection was running, and says so. On the IntoMind One each channel's bit is its positive electrode.

- npz and mat carry the lead-off byte for every sample and, beside it, whether detection was running at that sample.
- csv and tsv add a column per channel, `ch1_leadoff` and so on, with 1 where the electrode was off, 0 where it was attached, and empty where nothing was checking. The columns are present only when detection ran somewhere in the recording.
- bdf and edf label each stretch an electrode was off `BAD_LEADOFF` followed by the channel's label, which MNE treats as bad, and label the part of a recording where detection was off `LEADOFF_NOT_CHECKED`, written only when it ran for the rest.
- every export reports `contact`: `checked`, `partly checked`, `not checked`, or `not known` for a recording made before the flag was kept. bdf and edf also report `electrode_off_stretches`.

## Versions

The Python package, the Rust crates and the JavaScript package share one version number. Its minor digit follows the minor version of the protocol, so a package that speaks protocol 1.4 is a 1.4 release. Its last digit counts releases of the packages. A name that has been published, whether a function, a key in a summary, a column in a file or a field in a manifest, keeps its meaning in every later release. New names are added, old names are never removed or renamed. This site describes the released packages, and nothing newer.

<!-- https://docs.intomind.com/rust.html -->

# Rust

The `intomind` crate is a client for the IntoMind One that does no input or output of its own. You give it the bytes your Bluetooth stack received, and it returns events and the bytes to send. It works with any Bluetooth library and any async runtime, or none.

```sh
cargo add intomind
```

| Crate | |
|---|---|
| `intomind` | the client, with the timebase and head uploads |
| `intomind-protocol` | the protocol's messages as code. `no_std`, with no dependencies |
| `intomind-pipeline` | the device's processing chain, so a chain can be checked before it is sent |
| `intomind-model` | the encoder's arithmetic, as the device does it. `no_std`. Enable it with `--features model` |
| `intomind-capture` | recordings: recorded and read as every IntoMind program records and reads them, and exported in six formats |

## Connect and stream

Your Bluetooth library reads Device Info once, writes the commands the session builds, and passes every notification to the session.

```rust
use intomind::protocol::uuid_fill;
use intomind::{Event, Session};

fn stream(stack: &mut impl Stack) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let mut session = Session::new();
    session.on_device_info(&stack.read(uuid_fill::DEVICE_INFO)?)?;
    let info = *session.info()?;

    let start = session.start_stream();
    stack.write(start.characteristic, &start.bytes, start.with_response)?;

    while let Some((characteristic, bytes)) = stack.next_notification() {
        for event in session.on_notification(characteristic, &bytes) {
            match event {
                Event::Samples(batch) => {
                    for row in 0..batch.rows() {
                        let uv = batch.microvolts(row, 0, &info); // channel 1, in microvolts
                        println!("{} {uv:.2}", batch.index + row as u32);
                    }
                }
                // None when the device restarted its count.
                Event::Gap(gap) => println!("gap {:?}", gap.samples_lost),
                Event::Duplicate { .. } => {} // another program is listening: dropped
                _ => {}
            }
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}

/// What your Bluetooth library provides.
trait Stack {
    fn read(&mut self, fill: u16) -> Result<Vec<u8>, Box<dyn std::error::Error>>;
    fn write(&mut self, fill: u16, bytes: &[u8], with_response: bool) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>;
    fn next_notification(&mut self) -> Option<(u16, Vec<u8>)>;
}
```

`intomind::protocol::uuid128(fill)` gives each characteristic's full UUID.

## Commands

Every command is checked against what the device reported, and one the device cannot carry out returns an error rather than bytes.

```rust
use intomind::protocol::control::{indicator, mode};
use intomind::protocol::device_info::capability;

if session.can(capability::LEADOFF) {
    let command = session.set_leadoff(true)?;
}
// Every batch then says whether detection was running, in `batch.leadoff_active`:
// a lead-off byte of zero is an attached electrode only when it was.
let verbose = session.set_indicator(indicator::VERBOSE)?;          // silent, reserved, verbose
let identify = session.identify(5)?;                               // the status light winks for five seconds
let name = session.set_name("Ada", "Blue", "IntoMind One")?;       // refused unless it fits 29 bytes
let synthetic = session.set_mode(mode::SYNTHETIC)?;                // the generated signal
```

## Processing on the device

```rust
use intomind::protocol::pipeline::{kind, Chain, Stage};
use intomind::{Command, Error, Session};

fn my_chain(session: &Session) -> Result<Command, Error> {
    let mut chain = Chain::NATURAL;                    // no stages
    chain.push(Stage::one(kind::HIGH_PASS, 5))?;       // 0.5 Hz, in tenths of a hertz
    chain.push(Stage::two(kind::NOTCH, 580, 620))?;    // 58 to 62 Hz
    chain.push(Stage::one(kind::LOW_PASS, 0))?;        // the automatic corner
    session.set_pipeline(&chain, 500)                  // refused, with the reason, if it cannot run at 500
}
```

## Embeddings

```rust
use intomind::embeddings::{Assembler, Form};

let ask = session.set_embeddings(Some(Form::Window))?;
let mut windows = Assembler::new(4, 20, Form::Window);  // channels, tokens per channel
// for each Event::Embedding(part): if let Some(window) = windows.feed(part) { ... }
```

## Run your own head

A transfer tells you what to write, and you tell it what the device answered.

```rust
use intomind::{Step, Transfer};

let mut transfer = Transfer::head(&session, 2, &blob)?;   // slot 2: slot 1 holds the open sex head
loop {
    match transfer.step(&blob) {
        Step::Send(command) => {
            write(&command);
            transfer.on_answer(&update_answer()?, &blob)?;
        }
        Step::Data { from, to, .. } => {
            write_data(&blob[from..to]);
            transfer.sent(to - from);
        }
        Step::Verified(_) => break,
    }
}
```

Then select it with `session.select_head(2)` and turn predictions on with `session.set_predictions(true)`. Heads are trained in [Python](https://docs.intomind.com/python.html#the-model).

## The timebase

`Timebase` maps device time onto your computer's clock from time exchanges with the device. One exchange gives the offset between the clocks, and a rate needs at least three.

```rust
use intomind::{Exchange, Timebase};

let mut timebase = Timebase::new(info.time_tick_hz);
timebase.observe(Exchange { before, after, device_ticks });
let seconds = timebase.host_time(device_ticks);
```

The crates are tested against the protocol's conformance vectors, which the device's firmware generates from the code it runs.

## Record

The session records as the Python API records: the same four files, the same manifest, and the checksums written last, so a run that dies on the way is never taken for a whole recording. Its clock is the Python API's too. Give each time exchange both of your computer's clocks, read either side of it, and the session fits the device's time against the clock that never steps and holds the fit still while the device streams, so a recording's times never jump.

```rust
use intomind::capture::record::{Run, Setup};
use intomind::capture::recording::Collection;
use intomind::HostClocks;

// Each time exchange: send session.time_sync() and wait for its answer.
let before = HostClocks::now();
session.on_time_sync_clocks(&answer, before, HostClocks::now())?;

session.arm_recorder();             // then send reset_epoch() and start_stream()
// Every notification goes to session.on_notification, as before.
// Send stop_stream() at the end.
let mut run = Run::default();
run.extra.insert("experiment".into(), "my-experiment".into());
let recordings = Collection::open(Collection::default_dir());
let manifest = session.save_recording(&recordings, "my-recording", &Setup::default(), &run)?;
```

`Setup` declares what no code can discover: the adapter that carried the samples, facts about the hardware such as the mains frequency, and where the electrodes were put. What is not declared is written as unknown. A recording made here names the Rust crates as the software that made it, where one made by the Python API names Python. Everything else is the file the Python API writes from the same session.

## Recordings and exports

`intomind::capture` reads the recordings the Command Center and the Python API make, and exports them in the same six formats, with the same rules and the same summary. A BDF, EDF, CSV or TSV file exported here is the same file, byte for byte, as one exported from Python, and an NPZ or MATLAB file holds the same arrays.

```rust
use intomind::capture::{export, recording::Collection};

let recordings = Collection::open(Collection::default_dir());
let summary = export::export(&recordings, "my-recording", "bdf", None)?;   // also "edf", "npz", "csv", "tsv" and "mat"
println!("{} samples, largest error {} µV", summary["samples"], summary["max_error_uv"]);

let recording = recordings.load("my-recording")?;                       // refused if its checksums do not match
let ch1 = recording.uv(0)?;
```

`Collection::default_dir()` is the folder the Python API uses. An export with no path goes in `exports` beside it. What every file holds and promises is on [Recordings and files](https://docs.intomind.com/files.html).

## License

Free software under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3. For a commercial license, write to contact@intomind.com.

<!-- https://docs.intomind.com/javascript.html -->

# JavaScript

The `@intomind/sdk` package connects a web page to an IntoMind One over Web Bluetooth, with nothing for the user to install. It is written in TypeScript and also decodes the protocol in Node.

```sh
npm install @intomind/sdk
```

## Try it

With an IntoMind One switched on and unplugged, and a browser that has [Web Bluetooth](#browsers), you can connect to it from this page. Nothing is recorded, and nothing leaves your browser.

## Connect and stream

```ts
import { requestAndConnect } from "@intomind/sdk";

document.querySelector("#connect")?.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  const link = await requestAndConnect();              // the browser lists the devices nearby

  link.on((event) => {
    if (event.type === "samples") {
      const batch = event.batch;
      for (let row = 0; row < batch.rows; row++) {
        const uv = batch.microvolts(row, 0, link.info);  // channel 1, in microvolts
      }
    } else if (event.type === "gap") {
      console.log("lost", event.gap.samplesLost);        // null when the device restarted its count
    }
  });

  const answer = await link.request(link.session.startStream());
  if (!answer.ok) console.log("refused:", answer.statusName);
});
```

`requestAndConnect` must run from a click, on a page served over HTTPS or from `localhost`. The first connection pairs the device. `link.info` is what the device reported when it connected, and scaling a sample to microvolts needs it. Each batch carries the index and device time of its first sample, and a gap is announced before the batch that follows it.

Every batch says whether lead-off detection was running, in `batch.leadoffActive`, because a lead-off byte of zero is an attached electrode only when it was.

## Events

| Event | Carries |
|---|---|
| `samples` | samples, with `microvolts(row, channel, info)`, the first sample's index and device time, and whether the device generated them |
| `gap` | how many samples were lost, or `null` when the device restarted its count |
| `status` | battery, charger, whether USB is plugged in, and whether the device is streaming |
| `answer` | the device's answer to a command |
| `prediction` | a head's outputs for one window |
| `duplicate` | a packet that arrived twice and was dropped, because another program is listening to the device |

## Commands

`link.request` sends a command and waits for the device's answer. A command for something the device does not report is refused before it is sent.

```ts
import { protocol as P } from "@intomind/sdk";

const s = link.session;
await link.request(s.setRate(250));                     // refused while streaming
await link.request(s.setIndicator("verbose"));          // "silent", "reserved" or "verbose"
await link.request(s.identify(5));                      // the status light winks for five seconds
await link.request(s.setName("Ada", "Blue"));           // "Ada's Blue IntoMind One"
await link.request(s.setPipeline([P.highpass(0.5), ...P.mainsBands(60, 500), P.lowpass()], 500));
await link.request(s.setMode("synthetic"));             // the generated signal, at 500 per second
```

A stream started while USB is plugged in answers status 7: the device does not stream from its electrodes on USB power.

## Run your own head

Train a head in [Python](https://docs.intomind.com/python.html#the-model), then upload it from a page.

```ts
import { Transfer } from "@intomind/sdk";

const transfer = Transfer.head(link.session, 2, blob);   // slot 2: slot 1 holds the open sex head
await link.transfer(transfer, blob, ({ taken, total }) => console.log(`${taken} of ${total}`));
await link.request(link.session.selectHead(2));
await link.request(link.session.setPredictions(true));
```

## Browsers

Web Bluetooth is in Chrome on Windows, macOS, ChromeOS and Android, and in Edge and Opera on Windows and macOS. On Linux, Chrome needs `chrome://flags/#enable-web-bluetooth` turned on. Safari and Firefox do not have it, and neither does any browser on an iPhone or iPad.

## Node

Node has no Web Bluetooth, but everything except the connection works there. Pass the session the bytes your Bluetooth library receives, and write the bytes it returns.

```ts
import { Session, FILL } from "@intomind/sdk";

const session = new Session();
session.onDeviceInfo(deviceInfoBytes);                  // read from the Device Info characteristic
for (const event of session.onNotification(FILL.EEG_DATA, notificationBytes)) {
  // the same events as in a browser
}
const command = session.startStream();                  // write command.bytes to its characteristic
```

The package is tested against the protocol's conformance vectors, which the device's firmware generates from the code it runs.

## Record

The session records as the Python API records: the same four files, the same manifest, and the checksums written last, so a run that dies on the way is never taken for a whole recording. Its clock is the Python API's too. `link.timeSync()` reads both of your computer's clocks either side of each exchange, and the session fits the device's time against the clock that never steps and holds the fit still while the device streams, so a recording's times never jump.

```ts
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) await link.timeSync();   // a few exchanges before the stream

link.session.armRecorder();
await link.request(link.session.resetEpoch());
await link.request(link.session.startStream());
// the batches arrive as before
await link.request(link.session.stopStream());

const saved = link.session.saveRecording("my-recording", {}, { extra: { experiment: "my-experiment" } });
// saved.files holds each file's name and bytes: the npz, the manifest and the checksums
```

The second argument declares what no code can discover: the adapter that carried the samples, facts about the hardware such as the mains frequency, and where the electrodes were put. What is not declared is written as unknown. A recording made here names the JavaScript package as the software that made it. Everything else is the file the Python API writes from the same session.

In Node, give each time exchange both clocks yourself, read with `hostClocks()` from `@intomind/sdk/capture` either side of it, to `session.onTimeSyncClocks(answer, before, after)`. `writeRecording(defaultDir(), saved)` from `@intomind/sdk/capture/node` puts the files in the folder the Python API uses.

## Recordings and exports

`@intomind/sdk/capture` reads the recordings the Command Center and the Python API make, and exports them in the same six formats, with the same rules and the same summary. A BDF, EDF, CSV or TSV file exported here is the same file, byte for byte, as one exported from Python, and an NPZ or MATLAB file holds the same arrays. It reads and writes bytes, so it runs in a browser, with the files from a file picker or a download.

```ts
import { Collection, exportRecording } from "@intomind/sdk/capture";

const recordings = new Collection(files);                        // file name -> bytes
const bdf = exportRecording(recordings, "my-recording", "bdf");  // also "edf", "npz", "csv", "tsv" and "mat"
// bdf.bytes is the file, and bdf.summary what the Python API reports for it
```

In Node, `@intomind/sdk/capture/node` reads a folder and writes the export where the Python API would.

```ts
import { defaultDir, exportToFile, openCollection } from "@intomind/sdk/capture/node";

const summary = exportToFile(defaultDir(), "my-recording", "bdf");  // the folder the Python API uses
const recording = openCollection().load("my-recording");            // refused if its checksums do not match
```

What every file holds and promises is on [Recordings and files](https://docs.intomind.com/files.html).

## License

Free software under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3. For a commercial license, write to contact@intomind.com.

# MicroPython

MicroPython for the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W, with the `intomind` library built in, lets a program on the board connect to an IntoMind One with no computer in the room. It is MicroPython 1.29.0 as released for the Pico 2 W with pairing added, because the IntoMind One accepts commands and sends data only over a paired, encrypted link, and MicroPython as released cannot pair on the Pico 2 W. Everything else MicroPython does on the board, Wi-Fi included, works as usual.

## Install

1. Download `intomind-micropython-pico-2-w.uf2` from the `firmware` folder of [github.com/intomind/micropython](https://github.com/intomind/micropython).
2. Hold the BOOTSEL button while you plug the board into your computer, then let go. Drag the file onto the drive that appears.
3. The board restarts into MicroPython, and its banner reads `v1.29.0-intomind`. In Thonny, choose MicroPython (Raspberry Pi Pico) at the bottom right, and the prompt is the board's.

A program saved on the board as `main.py` runs whenever the board has power.

## Connect and stream

```micropython
import asyncio
import intomind


def on_packet(device, packet):
    scale = device.info.microvolts_per_count(packet.gain)
    channel_1 = [counts[0] * scale for counts in packet.counts]   # one count per channel in each row
    print(packet.index, channel_1)               # the first sample's index, and channel 1 in microvolts


async def main():
    device = await intomind.connect()            # the first IntoMind One heard
    print("Connected to", device.name)
    device.on_packet = on_packet                 # before start()
    await device.start()
    await asyncio.sleep(5)
    await device.stop()
    await device.disconnect()


asyncio.run(main())
```

`intomind.connect("Ada's")` connects to the first device whose name starts with `Ada's`, and `intomind.scan()` lists every device heard, the strongest first. The first connection pairs the board with the device, and later connections reuse the pairing, which the board keeps in `ble_secrets.json`. If a connection fails because the device no longer has the pairing, the error says to call `intomind.forget_pairings()`, and the next connection pairs again.

Each packet carries the index of its first sample. The next packet's index is this one's plus `packet.n_samples`, so a larger jump means samples were lost on the way. A stream started while the IntoMind One is plugged in is refused: `start()` raises `intomind.Refused` with status 7, because the device does not stream from its electrodes on USB power.

## What the device reports

The library holds no table of hardware. What a device can do is what it reports, and the methods for the battery, the model and heads raise `OSError` when it does not report that capability.

```micropython
device.info.channels                     # 4
device.info.rates                        # the sample rates it offers
device.can("heads")                      # True when it reports that capability
status = await device.read_status()      # streaming, battery, charger, USB, and contact
battery = await device.battery()         # millivolts, percent, and the charger
```

## Run a head

The IntoMind One runs heads on its own chip, and the board reads what they say. Train one in [Python](https://docs.intomind.com/python.html#the-model), or upload one from [JavaScript](https://docs.intomind.com/javascript.html#run-your-own-head).

```micropython
active, heads = await device.heads()
for head in heads:
    print(head.slot, head.name, head.state)      # "valid" when it can run


def on_prediction(device, p):
    if not (p.gap_in_window or p.leadoff_in_window):    # skip a window with a gap or an electrode off
        print(p.head_slot, p.outputs)


device.on_prediction = on_prediction
await device.select_head(2)                      # slot 2: slot 1 holds the open sex head
await device.start()
await device.set_predictions(True)
```

A program can then drive the board's pins from `p.outputs`, as a signal any circuit, robot or project of your own can act on.

## Requests

`device.command(name, arg)` sends any request in [the protocol](https://docs.intomind.com/protocol.html) by name and returns what the answer carries. A refusal raises `intomind.Refused`, with the status number in `status` and its name in `status_name`.

```micropython
await device.command("identify", 5)              # the status light winks for five seconds
await device.command("set_indicator", 2)         # verbose
```

`intomind.protocol` is the protocol on its own, in plain Python, for reading what an answer carries, such as `intomind.protocol.decode_battery(payload)`.

The library's tests read every message the way the published `@intomind/sdk` reads it.

## License

Free software under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3, with a permission to combine it with MicroPython and the libraries the firmware carries. For a commercial license, write to contact@intomind.com.

<!-- https://docs.intomind.com/model.html -->

# The model and heads

The IntoMind One runs a small neural network, an encoder, that reads 4 seconds of signal and describes it with 76 numbers, called an embedding. A head turns an embedding into the numbers you care about. You train heads on your own recordings, and the device runs them.

![The encoder on the device, and the heads around it](https://docs.intomind.com/assets/img/model.svg)

## Why it works this way

The encoder was trained on EEG from many people and many studies, so it describes EEG in general. It knows nothing about you or your question. A head is where your question goes: a small set of weights, trained on a laptop in seconds, that reads the embedding and produces up to 32 numbers. The device then runs it on every window.

A head is weights, never code. The device does not run code you send it.

## What ships

Every IntoMind One carries three open heads. Age is built into the model and selected when the device starts. Sex is in slot 1, one of the four slots that are yours. The reconstruction head is built into the model, where the device uses it for the [synthetic signal](https://docs.intomind.com/device.html#the-synthetic-signal).

Age and sex show what an embedding carries. They are not useful predictors of either. The heads and how they were measured are published at [github.com/intomind/eeg-foundation-model-heads](https://github.com/intomind/eeg-foundation-model-heads).

## Embeddings from the device

The device sends the encoder's output on request while it streams, in two forms:

- **The embedding**, 76 numbers per window. Heads read it, so train heads on it.
- **The tokens**, 80 vectors per window, one per channel for each fifth of a second. The embedding is their mean, and they turn back into signal.

```python
await device.start()
windows = await device.collect_embeddings(100, form="window")   # about seven minutes
tokens = await device.collect_embeddings(1, form="tokens")      # one window's tokens
```

Each window carries the index and device time of its first sample, so it lines up with your recording, and the identity of the encoder that produced it.

## Training a head

```python
from intomind.model import train_head

head = train_head([w.embedding for w in windows], targets, name="focus",
                  encoder_id=windows[0].encoder_id)
```

`train_head` fits a linear model with a ridge penalty that it chooses from your embeddings, and returns the head exactly as the device runs it. It refuses to fit unless there are more windows than the embedding has numbers. The embeddings you train on are the device's own, quantized as its heads receive them, so a head gives on your computer what it gives on the device.

## Running it on the device

```python
await device.upload_head(head, slot=2, select=True)    # slots 1 to 4 are yours; 1 holds the sex head
device.on_prediction = lambda dev, p: print(p.outputs)
await device.set_predictions(True)
```

The device checks a head's hash and its shape before it stores it. It never checks for a signature of ours, so you can run any head you train. A head records the encoder it was trained on, and the library and the Command Center warn you when it differs from the device's.

Each prediction names the head that made it and the index of the window's first sample, so predictions line up with the signal. It also says whether the window had a gap or an electrode off. The model runs only on time the stream does not need, so it never costs you samples.

The [JavaScript](https://docs.intomind.com/javascript.html#run-your-own-head) and [Rust](https://docs.intomind.com/rust.html#run-your-own-head) packages upload heads too.

## How often it runs

By default the model describes every window, a new one every 4 seconds. You can ask for one window every so many seconds instead, on a grid that starts with the stream. The device keeps the setting when it is turned off.

```python
interval = await device.model_interval()    # the interval in force, and the shortest the device allows
await device.set_model_interval(60)         # one window a minute; 0 is every window
```

## What the model reads

The model reads the stream: the processing chain's output, or the unfiltered signal when there is no chain. You can point it at the unfiltered signal or at a chain of its own without changing the stream, and every prediction says which it read. The model always works at 500 samples per second, from its own copy of the stream. The stream you receive is never resampled.

## Turning tokens back into signal

The open reconstruction head ships with the Python API and turns each token back into the fifth of a second it came from.

```python
from intomind.model import Reconstructor

reconstruct = Reconstructor.shipped()
window = (await device.collect_embeddings(1, form="tokens"))[0]
signal = reconstruct.from_tokens(window.tokens, channels=4, tokens_per_channel=20)   # (channels, samples)
```

What comes back is what the encoder kept of the window, in the model's normalized units. On windows from studies it was not fitted on, it returns about two thirds of the signal's variance: most of the rhythms below 13 Hz, less of those from 13 to 30 Hz, and little above 30 Hz. Windows with large artifacts do not come back in amplitude.

## The weights

The encoder's weights stay on the device. They arrive only in signed updates from IntoMind, cannot be read over the link, and are not published. Everything you work with is open: the embeddings and tokens the device sends, the heads you train, and the reconstruction head.

<!-- https://docs.intomind.com/protocol.html -->

# IntoMind BLE Protocol v1.4

Status: as built in firmware 1.4.2 and later. Units ship firmware 1.4.5,
2026-10-05, which also keeps every queued sample at a numbering restart.
Firmware 1.4.1 built all of it but section 27, and firmware 1.4.0,
2026-10-02, all but sections 26 and 27. It supersedes 1.3 under the
rules of section 0 of 1.1: a 1.3 host works against a 1.4 device, and a
1.4 host reads a 1.3 device's version and asks it nothing new.

What 1.4 adds:

- **USB power** (section 25): a device that is not run on its wearer while
  plugged in refuses to stream the natural signal while USB power is
  present, and stops a stream of it when USB power appears. The generated
  signal of section 22 still streams. One control status.
- **The heads' encoder ids in a request of their own** (section 26), so
  that every answer fits. One control opcode.
- **Every embedding notification within 156 bytes** (section 27), so that
  every notification but EEG Data fits the smallest MTU the contract
  allows, as section 3 of 1.0 has always said. No new number.

Two things defined earlier change. The LIST_HEADS trailer of 1.3 is
withdrawn, because with it the answer is longer than any answer may be,
and no device ever sent it (section 26.1). And the size of an embedding
notification, which section 19.2 of 1.2 tied to the negotiated MTU with a
wrong count, is now at most 156 bytes on every link (section 27). Nothing
else already defined in 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 changes meaning, size, or
number.

Device Info's `app_slot_bytes` and `weights_image_bytes` keep their
meaning. Firmware 1.4.0 divides its flash anew and reports 290816 and
401408 in them, where the field list of 1.0 shows the earlier
237568 and 507904. A host reads the two fields and never assumes them.

## Numbers assigned by 1.4

| Kind | Number | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Control status | 7 | refused while USB power is present, section 25 |
| Control opcode | 0x8A | LIST_HEAD_ENCODERS, section 26 |

None of these collides with a number in use or reserved (section 14 of
1.1, the numbers of 1.2 and 1.3). Control status 6 stays unassigned,
because the Update service answers 6 for a failed verification, and a
reader that sees both services should never meet one number with two
meanings.

## 25. USB power

The IntoMind One is not worn while it is plugged in. From 1.4 the device
holds to that itself: nothing that needs the device on someone's head runs
while USB power is present. USB power is what Status reports as
`usb_present`, flag bit 0.

### 25.1 What is refused

While `usb_present` is set, START_STREAM answers status 7 unless the
device is in the synthetic mode of section 22. That covers every mode that
reads the converter: the natural signal from the electrodes (mode 0), the
converter's own test signal (mode 1), and its shorted inputs (mode 2). The
converter is not started. Electrode contact quality and everything the
device computes from the natural signal ride on such a stream, so they do
not run either.

Settings are not refused: a host may choose a mode, a rate, a gain or a
chain while plugged in, and they take effect on the next stream.

Precedence, extending section 6 of 1.0: invalid argument, then
unsupported, then busy, then USB power, then hardware.

### 25.2 What stops

A stream of the natural signal that is running when USB power appears
ends at once. Its last sample is the last one converted before the device
saw USB power, and no sample after it is streamed. Samples already queued
are still sent, and every packet sent after the device saw USB power
carries `usb_present`, data flag bit 4, so a host can tell from the
packets alone. The next Status message, within one second, reads state 0
with `usb_present` set, and that pair is the reason. A host tells its user
to unplug to record. The samples streamed are complete and the stream
simply ends, so there is no gap inside it to mark. The device does not
resume when USB power goes away. A host starts a new stream.

### 25.3 What runs

The synthetic signal of section 22 streams while plugged in, with its
processing chain and the one model of section 22. So does everything that
does not read the electrodes: the connection, Device Info, settings, the
name, the lamp, updates, battery and charger state.

### 25.4 A 1.3 host

A 1.3 host does not know status 7. Under section 0 of 1.1 it treats any
status other than 0 as a refusal, so its user sees a stream that did not
start, or one that ended, with `usb_present` set in the same Status.

## 26. The heads' encoder ids

### 26.1 LIST_HEADS answers as it did in 1.2

1.3 appended to LIST_HEADS the encoder id each head names, one eight byte
id per record after the records (section 21.1 of 1.3). An IntoMind One
lists five records, the built-in slot and its four user slots, and with
the trailer that answer is 194 bytes. No answer on Control Response may be
longer than 156 bytes (section 3 of 1.0), so no device ever sent it:
firmware 1.3 and 1.4.0 answered LIST_HEADS with status 2.

From 1.4 LIST_HEADS answers exactly as in 1.2: `u8 active_slot, u8
n_entries`, then the records, and nothing after them. On the IntoMind One
the answer is 154 bytes. A 1.2 or 1.3 host parses it as it always has. The
encoder ids are in LIST_HEAD_ENCODERS.

### 26.2 LIST_HEAD_ENCODERS

| Opcode | Name | Arg | Response payload | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0x8A | LIST_HEAD_ENCODERS | | `u8 n_entries`, then `n_entries` records of 9 bytes | one record for each LIST_HEADS record, in the same order |

```
u8     slot
u8[8]  encoder_id   the id the head names, all zero for an empty slot or a head that does not say
```

On the IntoMind One the answer is 48 bytes. Without a model runtime the
request answers status 2, as LIST_HEADS does. A device before 1.4 answers
it with status 1, so a host asks it only of a device that reports 1.4 or
later.

A host does with these ids what section 21.1 of 1.3 says. A host that is
refused this request knows nothing of which encoder the heads name, and
shows each head as it shows one that does not say.

### 26.3 Every answer fits

No answer on Control Response, at its largest, is longer than 156 bytes.
A device that fails to compose an answer, which a device that keeps to
this contract never does, answers status 5. It never answers status 2,
which says the device does not do what was asked, and never answers
status 0 with less than the whole answer. The same holds on Update
Control, where the status is 5 as well.

## 27. Embedding notifications fit 156 bytes

Section 3 of 1.0 holds every notification and indication but EEG Data to
156 bytes, so that an MTU of 159, the smallest the contract allows for
them, carries each one whole. Section 19.2 of 1.2 said instead that an
embedding notification carries as many values as fit the negotiated MTU,
and that 96 values fit at that smallest MTU. The count is wrong: after the
28 byte header, 64 values fit. And firmware 1.2 to 1.4.1 kept neither
rule. It filled a part with up to 108 values, 244 bytes, whatever the MTU,
so the launch model's 76 value vectors each went as one notification of
180 bytes, which a host below an MTU of 183 received cut short.

From 1.4, as built in firmware 1.4.2, an embedding notification carries at
most 64 values, 156 bytes, on every link. A vector wider than that goes in
parts exactly as section 19.2 of 1.2 defines: each part names its `first`
value, and every part but the last sets `more_parts`. The launch model's
vectors go in two parts, 64 values and 12. A host puts parts back together
as it always has, so a 1.2 or 1.3 host reads them unchanged, and a
notification from an earlier firmware reads as it did.

No number is assigned, and nothing else changes.

<!-- https://docs.intomind.com/safety.html -->

# Safety and care

## Not a medical device

The IntoMind One is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease or condition. It is a research and development instrument. Nothing it records or reports is a clinical measurement, and nothing on this site is medical advice. You use it at your own risk.

## Who should not use it

- Infants, young children, and anyone with a weak or sensitive scalp.
- Anyone with an implanted electrical device, such as a pacemaker, a neurostimulator, or a cochlear implant, without first asking the doctor who manages it.
- Anyone with broken or irritated skin where the electrodes would rest.

## While you wear it

The device is designed to be safe against a single electrical fault on battery power only. To ensure safety, never wear it or touch its electrodes while USB is plugged in.

Do not use it in wet or damp conditions, or while driving, operating machinery, or doing anything else where a distraction could cause harm.

The electrodes only measure, except when you turn on lead-off detection, which passes a very small current through them. Take the device off if the skin under an electrode becomes sore or red.

## The battery

The device has a lithium polymer battery. Treat it as you would the battery in a phone.

- Charge it from an ordinary USB charger or computer.
- Do not charge it unattended on a soft surface.
- Do not puncture or crush the device.
- If the device becomes hot, swells, or smells, stop using it, move it away from anything that can burn, and do not charge it again.
- Do not put it in household waste. Take it to a battery recycling point.

## Cleaning

With the power off, charger disconnected, and ideally the battery disconnected as well, wipe the electrodes with a damp cloth and let them dry. Do not use solvents, alcohol or abrasives on them.

Do not submerge the device or hold it under running water. It is not sealed.

## Storage

Store the device dry and charged. The battery drains slowly even while the device is off, and a lithium battery left empty for a long time may not recover.

## Your recordings

Recordings are written to your own computer. The Command Center and the Python API send nothing over the internet and need no account. A recording of brain activity is personal data, so share one only on purpose.

<!-- https://docs.intomind.com/glossary.html -->

# Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ADC | The analog-to-digital converter, which turns the electrodes' voltages into numbers. The IntoMind One uses a Texas Instruments ADS1299-4. |
| API | The Python package `intomind`, for scripts, recordings and analysis. |
| Capability | A feature a device reports that it supports. Software asks a device only for what it reports. |
| Channel | One electrode, measured against the reference. The IntoMind One has four. |
| Command Center | The app for using the device from your computer, in your browser. |
| Device time | The device's own clock, which stamps every sample. Software maps it onto your computer's clock. |
| Embedding | The 76 numbers the encoder produces for each window. Heads read them. |
| Encoder | The neural network on the device that produces embeddings and tokens. |
| Filter | A high-pass filter removes slow drift, a low-pass filter removes fast content, and a notch filter removes a narrow band, such as the mains frequency. |
| Gain | How much the ADC amplifies the signal before converting it, from 1 to 24. |
| Gap | A place in a stream where samples were lost. The stream says where and how many. |
| Generator | The small model on the device that produces the synthetic signal. |
| Head | A small set of weights that turns an embedding into up to 32 numbers. You train heads and run them on the device. |
| Lead-off detection | A check that shows which electrodes touch the skin, by passing a very small current through them. |
| Mains frequency | The frequency of household electricity, 50 or 60 Hz, which every EEG picks up. |
| Pairing | The first connection between a computer and the device, which sets up the encryption for every later one. |
| Placeholder | A value written in a BDF or EDF file where a sample was lost, repeating the last recorded value, under the label that marks the hole. |
| Processing chain | The filters the device applies to its signal before streaming it. Every stream states its chain. |
| Protocol | The contract for the Bluetooth messages between an IntoMind device and any software. |
| Reconstruction head | The open head that turns tokens back into signal. |
| Recording | The samples, the manifest, the markers and the checksums that one capture session wrote, kept together under one name. |
| Reference | The electrode every channel is measured against. |
| Sample | One measurement of every channel at one moment. |
| Sample rate | How many samples the device takes per second: 250, 500 or 1000. |
| SDK | The Rust crates and the JavaScript package for building your own applications. |
| Slot | One of four places on the device for a head you upload. |
| Synthetic signal | A signal the device generates in place of its electrodes, marked as generated wherever it goes. |
| Token | One of the 80 vectors the encoder produces for each window, one per channel for each fifth of a second. |
| Web Bluetooth | The browser feature that lets a web page connect to a Bluetooth device. |
| Window | Four seconds of signal, the span the model describes at once. |
| µV | A microvolt, one millionth of a volt. EEG is measured in microvolts. |
